findings.breaking_input: upstream repo id = "owner/name\n" (a valid owner/name followed by a newline)
findings.why: repo()'s regex is not anchored with ^...$, so an id with a trailing newline or other suffix passes. The id is interpolated raw into API URL paths, so the newline and any following text alter the request target. ADR-1726's promise that upstream is exactly one repo shaped owner/name is not enforced.
findings.fix: Anchor the regex with ^...$ and reject any id that is not exactly owner/name; also encodeURIComponent each path segment before interpolating it into the URL.
findings.twin_of: Upstream entries were coerced with String(), so a `null` id became the hostname "null"

findings.breaking_input: A real GitHub Actions run that stays queued/in_progress longer than 12×20 seconds (e.g. a cold macOS job taking 6 minutes)
findings.why: verify() polls 12 times and then reports 'no run of arc-ci on main yet', which is a false negative: the run exists and is still running. The loop conflates 'run not created yet' with 'run not completed yet', and the 240s cap is far too short for cold GitHub-hosted runners.
findings.fix: After the poll budget, return ok:false with reason 'run N still <status>' instead of 'no run', and distinguish an empty workflow_runs list from a non-completed run.
findings.twin_of: A sleep listened for "abort" on a signal that had already fired

findings.breaking_input: Upstream repo id = "owner/na%2Fme" (percent-encoded slash inside the name segment)
findings.why: The id passes the unanchored owner/name regex (the regex sees 'name' after a slash and permits the encoded characters as a later substring). Since no encodeURIComponent is applied to `full`, the encoded slash is sent to the API as a path separator, changing which API resource is addressed.
findings.fix: Anchor the full-match regex and encodeURIComponent the owner and name separately before building /repos/{owner}/{name} paths.
findings.twin_of: The adapter path was data the runner trusted

findings.breaking_input: Scenario 'owner-edited' where the hand-edited file is replaced by any content starting with '# Written by arc launch', even if the rest of the file differs from WORKFLOW
findings.why: The test asserts out.restored is true only if the rewritten content starts with the header comment. It never asserts the content is byte-identical to WORKFLOW, nor that the latest commit message contains Arc-Launch-Tag. A regression that truncates or alters the workflow would still pass.
findings.fix: Assert the decoded file equals WORKFLOW exactly and that the commit message contains `Arc-Launch-Tag: <tag>`.
findings.twin_of: A test titled "only those" had nothing it could have leaked

findings.breaking_input: A 403 from an endpoint other than branch protection whose message contains 'Upgrade to GitHub Pro' (e.g. a rate-limit or abuse message that happen to include that phrase)
findings.why: The PLAN_LIMIT classifier matches any 403 whose message contains that phrase, regardless of the request path. A 403 from GET /repos or from the workflow-runs endpoint would be misreported as the ADR-1726 plan limit instead of the real error.
findings.fix: Only map that phrase to PLAN_LIMIT when the failing request was PUT /repos/{owner}/{name}/branches/main/protection.
findings.twin_of: Provider error text and resolver answers went raw into the slot's reason

findings.breaking_input: A workflow run whose `head_sha` is on a non-main branch (e.g. a pull_request run) while the main branch has no run
findings.why: The fake ignores the `branch=main` query parameter and always returns the most recent run regardless of branch. verify() then sees a completed run with green legs and returns ok:true even though main has never run the workflow. The real GitHub API honors the branch filter, so the contract test can pass while the real adapter would fail.
findings.fix: Honor the branch query parameter in the fake, and add a scenario where the only run is on a non-main branch; verify() must return ok:false.
findings.twin_of: `verify` re-implemented apply's checks and kept only half

findings.breaking_input: POST /user/repos returns 422 (concurrent creation), then the follow-up GET returns 404 because the other creator deleted the repo between the two calls
findings.why: The 422 fallback path calls own() on the follow-up GET without checking its status. A 404 body is passed to own(), which throws a generic 'github returned no repo for ...' error instead of the explicit UPSTREAM_MISSING/FOREIGN_REPO style refusal the lane uses. It is still a refusal, but the wrong code propagates.
findings.fix: After the 422 fallback GET, treat a 404 as UPSTREAM_MISSING and otherwise apply the same own() judgment as the normal path.
findings.twin_of: An unrecorded sensitive-action request left the slot "awaiting" an id that did not exist

findings.breaking_input: A GitHub response whose JSON body is `{ "workflow_runs": null }` with HTTP 200
findings.why: list(runs.body.workflow_runs) treats null as [] and the loop prints 'no run of arc-ci on main yet'. An anomalous 200 body is silently converted into a false negative instead of a transport/provider error, masking API changes or bugs.
findings.fix: Guard with `Array.isArray(runs.body && runs.body.workflow_runs)` and throw a parse error otherwise.
findings.twin_of: `errors || []` trusted the provider to send an array of objects

findings.breaking_input: A GITHUB_TOKEN of exactly 20 characters like `gho_1234567890123456`
findings.why: The token shape regex /^[A-Za-z0-9_]{20,}$/ accepts a 20-character dummy, which real GitHub tokens never are (they are longer and carry a prefix like gho_, ghp_, github_pat_). The adapter then reports a generic 401 instead of BAD_TOKEN, making misconfiguration harder to diagnose.
findings.fix: Require GitHub's actual token prefix and length, e.g. /^(gho|ghp|github_pat)_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,}$/.
findings.twin_of: A token with a CR reached a fetch header

findings.breaking_input: A workflow run that completes with the three check names present plus an extra required check (e.g. a third-party status check the owner added)
findings.why: verify() only checks that the three contexts are in the required list, not that the required list contains exactly the three checks. ADR-1726's 'requires its three checks' permits extras, so a main branch that requires four checks returns ok:true. This is arguably acceptable, but it is a silent divergence from the ADR's wording and could let an owner's extra requirement go unnoticed.
findings.fix: Either document that extras are allowed, or fail when contexts.length !== CHECKS.length.
